> **▶ [Solve it on TrueInterview](https://trueinterview.io/questions/service-shutdown-topological-sort)** — free, no card: a runnable editor, the sample and hidden tests, a judged verdict, and the reference solution.

## Problem

## Requirements

- Input: a graph of service dependencies; you are expected to settle on a representation with the interviewer, and `hashmap<service, list<dependents>>` is a typical choice.
- The graph is promised to contain no cycles, but verify that assumption aloud before you begin implementation.
- Given an initial collection of stopped services, produce all services that rely on any stopped service, whether the reliance is immediate or through a chain.

## Examples

Using edges written as (consumer → dependency):

```
M -> N
P -> N
Q -> P
```

If `N` is shut down, the result is `{M, P, Q}` because Q relies on P, and P in turn relies on N.

## Notes

- Clarifications are part of the evaluation: ask about the graph encoding, whether cycles can occur, duplicate entries, and whether initially shut-down services belong in the returned set.

## Preparation

- Work through LeetCode 207 (Course Schedule) and 210 (Course Schedule II) until Kahn-based and DFS-based solutions feel automatic.
- Rehearse a one-minute clarification checklist covering representation, edge orientation, cycles, duplicates, result format, and boundary cases such as an empty seed set or every service being stopped.
- Be ready with an OOD-oriented restatement: model a `Service` with `name` and `depends_on`, then expose a `shutdown(services)` operation that returns the impacted services.
- Practice this one-minute opening as a script: "Which way do edges point? Is the graph guaranteed cycle-free? Should the seed services appear in the result? Can inputs contain duplicates? What should happen for an empty seed set?"

### Canonical "Course Schedule" framing

- In VO terminology, the prompt may be presented merely as a "topological sort" instead of a service-shutdown scenario. Before selecting BFS, DFS, or Kahn, clarify edge direction, the requested output, and whether the goal is an ordering, reachability result, or cycle test.

## Hints

<details>
<summary>Hint 1</summary>

Think of the dependency graph as a DAG where a service can only be shut down after all its dependents have been removed.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Hint 2</summary>

Use a topological sort in reverse order, starting from the leaf nodes (services with no dependents) and working backward.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Hint 3</summary>

The tricky edge case is when the initial set of stopped services is empty, you must still produce a valid shutdown order for all services.

</details>
